finding.title: UnixFileLock opens lock file with O_TRUNC without O_NOFOLLOW, allowing symlink attack to truncate/overwrite arbitrary files
finding.evidence: Caller-supplied path reaches `os.open` unguarded. `BaseFileLock.__init__` (filelock/_api.py:184) stores `os.fspath(lock_file)`; `acquire()` (filelock/_api.py:332) calls `self._acquire()`. In `UnixFileLock._acquire`, `ensure_directory_exists(self.lock_file)` (line 40) creates the lock's directory, then `open_flags = os.O_RDWR | os.O_TRUNC` (line 41) and `fd = os.open(self.lock_file, open_flags, self._context.mode)` (line 44) are used. The flags contain no `os.O_NOFOLLOW`, and `os.open` follows symbolic links on the final path component. When the lock file lives in a shared/world-writable location (the common case, e.g. a /tmp or cache directory, or any dir the attacker can write to), an attacker can pre-plant a symlink at `lock_file` pointing at a victim-owned file; the victim process then opens the symlink target with O_TRUNC, zeroing that file (e.g. ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, application config/state, DB files) and the follow-up `os.fchmod(fd, self._context.mode)` (line 46) rewrites its permissions. `Path(self.lock_file).exists()` (line 42) is also link-following, so a dangling symlink causes `O_CREAT` to be added and the process writes/creates a file at the attacker-chosen target. No `lstat`/`O_NOFOLLOW`/`follow_symlinks=False` check exists anywhere in the acquisition path, so link following is unconditional; the reference (fixed) implementation adds `os.O_NOFOLLOW` to this open and switches the pre-check to `lstat`, confirming the missing protection.

finding.title: WindowsFileLock opens lock file with O_TRUNC and follows reparse points (symlink/junction) to arbitrary files
finding.evidence: On win32 the default `FileLock` maps to `WindowsFileLock` (filelock/__init__.py). `acquire()` (filelock/_api.py:332) invokes `_acquire()`, which builds `flags = os.O_RDWR | os.O_CREAT | os.O_TRUNC` (lines 22-26) and calls `fd = os.open(self.lock_file, flags, self._context.mode)` (line 28) with no reparse-point protection (no `FILE_FLAG_OPEN_REPARSE_POINT`/`NtCreateFile` and no `GetFileInformationByHandle` reparse-tag check). The `lock_file` argument is attacker-influenceable whenever the lock sits in a directory a lower-privileged user can write to; a reparse point (symlink, or a junction/mount point that an unprivileged user can create without SeCreateSymbolicLinkPrivilege) planted at that path is transparently followed by `os.open`, so the O_TRUNC open truncates the link target (any file the victim process can write) and `msvcrt.locking(fd, msvcrt.LK_NBLCK, 1)` (line 34) then locks it. The path is used directly with no `lstat`/reparse check, so following is unconditional; the fixed reference implementation opens via `NtCreateFile` with `FILE_OPEN_REPARSE_POINT` and explicitly rejects reparse points ('Lock file is a reparse point (symlink/junction)'), confirming the missing mitigation.

finding.title: UnixFileLock follows a symlink at the lock path and truncates/chmods the symlink target (arbitrary file destruction)
finding.evidence: UnixFileLock._acquire() builds open_flags = os.O_RDWR | os.O_TRUNC (line 41, adding os.O_CREAT at line 43 only when Path(self.lock_file).exists() is false) and then calls os.open(self.lock_file, open_flags, self._context.mode) at line 44, immediately followed by os.fchmod(fd, self._context.mode) at line 46. No O_NOFOLLOW flag and no lstat()/inode verification is used anywhere on this path: the existence probe at line 42 and ensure_directory_exists() at line 40 both resolve symlinks rather than rejecting them. An attacker who can create an entry at the lock-file path (lock file in a shared or attacker-writable directory, e.g. /tmp or a multi-tenant workspace) just plants a symlink lock_path -> victim_file. When the victim runs UnixFileLock(lock_path).acquire()/with-lock, os.open() resolves the link and, because O_TRUNC is set, truncates the victim file to zero bytes (integrity/availability loss); the subsequent os.fchmod(fd, const mode) rewrites the victim's permission bits to the caller's mode (default 0o644), which can widen access on a previously owner-only file (confidentiality loss). The destructive open happens before fcntl.flock() is attempted at line 48, so even a process that fails to obtain the lock still truncates the target. The same unprotected open-the-lock-path pattern is used by WindowsFileLock._acquire and SoftFileLock._acquire (the latter only partially shielded because O_CREAT|O_EXCL raises EEXIST on a symlink on Linux). Later hardened revisions of this module add O_NOFOLLOW to the open flags and defer truncation/fchmod until after flock succeeds, confirming the missing link-following protection is the root cause rather than intended behavior.

finding.title: Double free/double drop in ThinVec::clear() when an element's Drop panics
finding.evidence: Reachable from entirely safe code. `ThinVec::clear()` (lines 1082-1087) does `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut self[..])` and only afterwards `self.set_len(0)`. `T` is a generic caller-chosen type, so any element's `Drop` may panic (very common: a `Drop` that validates/parses/locks/asserts on attacker-influenced data). When that panic unwinds out of `drop_in_place`, execution never reaches the `set_len(0)` on line 1085, so the `ThinVec` still reports its original length while some of its elements have already been dropped. The `ThinVec`'s own destructor then runs during unwind: `Drop for ThinVec` (line 1912 -> 1917) calls `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut this[..])` again over the unchanged length, re-dropping elements whose `Drop` already completed. For any resource-owning `T` (e.g. fields of type `Box`/`Vec`/`String`), the same allocation is released twice, i.e. a double free / use-after-free (CWE-415), plus re-running arbitrary user `Drop` code. There is no guard or check on the panic path that resets the length. Required configuration: default `std` build with the normal `panic = "unwind"` strategy. This is the known issue fixed upstream in thin-vec 0.2.16; inspected 0.2.21 source wraps `clear` in a `DropGuard` whose `Drop` calls `set_len(0)` even when element dropping panics, and its RELEASES.md states: "Fix two double-drop issues with ThinVec::clear() and ThinVec::into_iter() when the Drop implementation of the item panics."

finding.title: Double free/double drop in IntoIter::drop when an element's Drop panics
finding.evidence: Reachable from safe code. `Drop for IntoIter<T>` (lines 2539-2556) calls the helper `drop_non_singleton` (line 2544), which does `let mut vec = mem::replace(&mut this.vec, ThinVec::new());` (line 2546, taking ownership of the inner `ThinVec` into a local), then `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut vec[this.start..])` (line 2547) and finally `vec.set_len_non_singleton(0)` (line 2548). If any element's `Drop` for the generic caller-supplied `T` panics, line 2548 is skipped and unwinding drops the local `vec`, whose `Drop for ThinVec` (line 1912) runs `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut this[..])` over the still-unmodified length (`start` is not accounted for), re-dropping elements that were already dropped, including `vec[0..start]` which were never owned by the iterator anyway. For resource-owning `T` this frees the same allocation twice (double free / use-after-free, CWE-415) and re-runs arbitrary user `Drop` code; the missing protection is that the length is only cleared after the fallible `drop_in_place` returns. Minimal reachability: `let mut v = ThinVec::new(); v.push(resource_owning_T); drop(v.into_iter());` where that element's `Drop` panics, in a default `std` build using `panic = "unwind"`. Upstream fixed exactly this in thin-vec 0.2.16 by adding a `DropGuard` in `IntoIter`'s drop helper; the inspected 0.2.21 sources show the guard calling `set_len_non_singleton(0)` on unwind, and the RELEASES.md for 0.2.16 records it as one of the "two double-drop issues".

finding.title: Double free / use-after-free in ThinVec::clear when an element's Drop panics
finding.evidence: ThinVec::clear (lines 1082-1087) drops every element and only then resets the length: `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut self[..])` at line 1084 runs the element destructors over the slice sized by the current, non-zero `self.len()`, and `self.set_len(0)` at line 1085 is expected to mark the storage empty. No panic guard protects that ordering. If any element's Drop panics (a realistic scenario for attacker-influenced data or any type whose Drop can panic), the unwind aborts `drop_in_place` and line 1085 is never executed, so the header still records the original length even though some/all elements were already destroyed. The ThinVec is now in a state where its length claims live elements over freed storage. When the vector is subsequently dropped, `ThinVec::drop` (line 1917 `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut this[..])`) re-runs destructors over the same still-reported length, double-dropping the already-freed elements; likewise a second `clear()`/`truncate()` re-drops them. This yields a double free / use-after-free of the element allocations, i.e. memory corruption reachable from ordinary safe API usage with default crate features. The upstream project later fixed exactly this by wrapping the vector in a DropGuard that resets the length even on unwind (0.2.16: 'Fix two double-drop issues with ThinVec::clear() ... when the Drop implementation of the item panics'); the code under audit lacks that guard, so the protection is absent.

finding.title: Double free / use-after-free in IntoIter::drop when an element's Drop panics
finding.evidence: ThinVec::into_iter produces IntoIter{vec,start}. On drop, `drop_non_singleton` (line 2544) takes ownership with `let mut vec = mem::replace(&mut this.vec, ThinVec::new())` (line 2546), drops the not-yet-yielded elements via `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut vec[this.start..])` (line 2547), and only then zeroes the length with `vec.set_len_non_singleton(0)` (line 2548). If any element's Drop panics, line 2548 is skipped and unwinding drops the local `vec` value, invoking `ThinVec::drop` (line 1917 `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut this[..])`) over the entire, still non-zero `vec.len()` — including the elements that were just destroyed. That is a double free / use-after-free of the moved-out elements. Trigger: collect elements into a ThinVec, make one of the later elements panic in Drop, start consuming with `into_iter()` (or simply drop the IntoIter after advancing past the earlier elements); the panic during the iterator's drop re-drops the already-freed items. As with clear(), no DropGuard/panic guard exists on this path; the upstream 0.2.16 release fixed it by installing a DropGuard that clears the length even during unwinding ('Fix two double-drop issues with ... ThinVec::into_iter() when the Drop implementation of the item panics'). This is reachable with default features through safe iterator APIs.

finding.title: Missing-signature rejection skipped when key is empty, allowing unsigned token acceptance
finding.evidence: verifyToken computes `hasKey = key instanceof Buffer ? key.length : !!key` (line 180). When the verifier is constructed with an empty secret (`key: ''`), hasKey is false, so the guard `if (hasKey && !signature)` at line 182 never throws missingSignature, and the second branch `else if (!hasKey && signature)` (line 184) is not taken for a token that has no signature. Control then reaches validateAlgorithmAndSignature, where the signature is verified only when it is truthy (`if (signature && !verifySignature(header.alg, key, input, signature))`, line 139); an empty signature segment therefore skips signature verification entirely, leaving only the `allowedAlgorithms.includes(header.alg)` check (line 134). With the common configuration `createVerifier({ key: '', algorithms: ['HS256'] })` (e.g. a blank/empty secret supplied via an environment variable), this check passes, so an unauthenticated attacker who submits `base64url({"alg":"HS256"}).base64url({"sub":"admin"}).` (empty signature segment) receives the attacker-chosen payload. Reproduced locally against src/verifier.js: the call returned {"sub":"admin"}. No key material is required to exploit it; the only prerequisite is that the configured key resolves to an empty string while an `algorithms` list is set.

finding.title: Unrecognized asymmetric key material is silently treated as an HMAC secret, enabling algorithm confusion
finding.evidence: performDetectPublicKeyAlgorithms classifies any key that is not a recognized PEM or X.509 certificate as a plain shared secret (`else if (!publicKeyPemMatch && !key.includes(publicKeyX509CertMatcher)) { return hsAlgorithms }`, lines 133-136). verifier.js then adopts that classification (`allowedAlgorithms = availableAlgorithms`, lines 406/347) and wraps the supplied bytes as an HMAC key via `prepareKeyOrSecret(currentKey, availableAlgorithms[0] === hsAlgorithms[0])` (line 350), so HS256/384/512 tokens are validated with the byte string of a key that is actually public/symmetric-asymmetric material. Because the public key is known to any attacker, this is a signature-forgery / algorithm-confusion authentication bypass whenever the verification key is supplied in a non-PEM form (e.g. a DER/SPKI Buffer or JWKS bytes). Reproduced locally: constructing `createVerifier({ key: publicKey.export({type:'spki',format:'der'}) })` and verifying an HS256 token whose HMAC key is exactly those DER bytes returned {"sub":"admin","iss":"app"}; the same forged token was accepted through the async key-function path (`key: (d,cb)=>cb(null,der)`). The library never rejects the downgrade to HMAC, so the attacker does not need the private key.

finding.title: Unvalidated Blake2b key length causes stack buffer overflow
finding.evidence: blake2b() takes an arbitrary-length `key` and calls crypto_blake2b_keyed(hash, len(hash), key, len(key), msg, len(msg)) at line 281; Blake2b.__init__ does the same via crypto_blake2b_keyed_init(&self._ctx, self._hash_size, key, len(key)) at line 297. Neither path validates the key length anywhere (lines 276-297). In the called C code, monocypher.c:544-546 declares a fixed `u8 key_block[128]` and copies key_size bytes into it with the byte-wise COPY macro (`#define COPY(dst,src,size) FOR(_i_,0,size) (dst)[_i_]=(src)[_i_]`), so a key longer than 128 bytes writes past the 128-byte stack buffer (stack canary/return address corruption). The attacker only needs to control the `key` argument length; no other precondition exists. Confirmed against the compiled binding: blake2b(b'msg', key=b'A'*32) returns a hash, while blake2b(b'msg', key=b'A'*200) aborts the interpreter before returning, consistent with stack corruption.

finding.title: Unchecked malloc result in argon2i_32 leads to NULL pointer dereference
finding.evidence: argon2i_32() (lines 322-352) uses the caller-supplied `nb_blocks` directly: config.nb_blocks = nb_blocks (line 328) and work_area = malloc((<size_t> nb_blocks) * (<size_t> 1024)) (line 345). Unlike password/salt/key/ad, `nb_blocks` is never passed through _validate_u32, and the malloc return value is never checked for NULL. Any nb_blocks value that fits uint32 but makes the (up to ~4 TB) allocation fail yields work_area == NULL, which is then handed to crypto_argon2(hash, 32, work_area, ...) at line 347; monocypher.c:914-915 executes ZERO(p, 128*nb_blocks) (with p = (u64*)work_area) through that NULL pointer, crashing the process. Confirmed: argon2i_32(4294967295, 1, b'pw', b'salt123456789012') segfaults (SIGSEGV) the interpreter with no Python exception, i.e. it is a reachable availability violation from ordinary API input.

finding.title: Unvalidated BLAKE2b key length overflows fixed 128-byte stack buffer in crypto_blake2b_keyed_init
finding.evidence: blake2b() (lines 276-282) and Blake2b.__init__ (lines 294-297) pass the caller-supplied key together with len(key) straight to Monocypher: crypto_blake2b_keyed(hash, len(hash), key, len(key), msg, len(msg)) at line 281 and crypto_blake2b_keyed_init(&self._ctx, self._hash_size, key, len(key)) at line 297. No check limits key_size (Monocypher's contract is key_size <= 64), and Cython emits no size validation for the `const uint8_t* key` parameter - the generated c_monocypher.c only does `__Pyx_PyObject_AsUString(key)` (a bare pointer to the bytes buffer), so an arbitrary-length bytes object is accepted. In the vendored monocypher.c:544-546 crypto_blake2b_keyed_init executes `u8 key_block[128] = {0}; COPY(key_block, key, key_size);`, i.e. a memcpy of key_size bytes into a 128-byte stack buffer. Any key longer than 128 bytes (e.g. an application that MACs with a key/password supplied by the user) therefore produces a stack out-of-bounds write with attacker-controlled length and contents, smashing the stack cookie/return address (memory corruption, potential code execution). Reachability was confirmed from the inspected binding and monocypher.c; a runnable PoC could not be built locally because no C toolchain is installed.

finding.title: argon2i_32 does not validate nb_blocks: undersized heap work area, out-of-bounds argon2 blocks, unchecked malloc
finding.evidence: argon2i_32 (lines 322-352) copies the caller-controlled nb_blocks directly into config.nb_blocks (line 328) and allocates work_area = malloc((<size_t> nb_blocks) * 1024) (line 345) without enforcing Monocypher's requirement nb_blocks >= 8*nb_lanes, and without checking that malloc succeeded (lines 345-349). In monocypher.c:752-754 the effective block count is rounded down: segment_size = config.nb_blocks / config.nb_lanes / 4 and lane_size = segment_size * 4, so for nb_blocks in 0..3 the effective nb_blocks/lane_size become 0. The lane-initialisation loop at monocypher.c:776-783 nevertheless unconditionally writes blocks[l*lane_size + i] for i in {0,1}, i.e. blocks[0] and blocks[1] = 2048 bytes, independent of the allocation: nb_blocks=1 allocates only 1024 bytes and then writes 2048 (heap overflow), nb_blocks=0 calls malloc(0) and then writes 2048. Line 902 (blk *last_block = blocks + lane_size - 1) additionally reads blocks[-1] out of bounds, and line 915 wipes 128*0 bytes. A very large nb_blocks makes malloc return NULL, which crypto_argon2 dereferences as `blocks` (NULL-pointer write). An attacker who controls the argon2 parameters (nb_blocks taken from untrusted configuration/data instead of a fixed constant) can therefore corrupt the heap or crash the process.

finding.title: ChunkedReader accepts malformed chunk footers (unvalidated 2-byte discard), enabling HTTP request smuggling
finding.evidence:
Attacker-controlled chunked body bytes reach ChunkedReader.__call__. After a chunk's data is consumed, the reader records only a length (self._bytes_to_discard = 2 at line 197, set in the header comment as 'throw away the trailing 
') and on the next call extracts that many bytes and drops them at line 167 with `self._bytes_to_discard -= len(data)` — no comparison against b"
" is ever performed (the block at lines 163-169 only checks that the count reached zero). Flow: request/response headers select the "chunked" reader via READERS (line 243) -> Connection dispatches into ChunkedReader -> line 164 `buf.maybe_extract_at_most(self._bytes_to_discard)` returns the two footer bytes -> line 167 discards them unconditionally -> parsing continues as if a valid CRLF footer was seen. PoC (poc_chunk_footer.py) drives h11 0.14.0 with `5
helloXX0

`, `5
hello X0

`, and `5
hello
X0

`; all are ACCEPTED and yield Data(b'hello') + EndOfMessage, whereas the patched 0.16.0 raises RemoteProtocolError('malformed chunk footer ... expected b"\r\n"') for the same input. This missing-protection laxity (CVE-2025-43859, GHSA-vqfr-h8mv-ghfj) makes h11's chunk framing disagree with intermediaries/peers that require CRLF footers, allowing a desync/smuggled request; requires only that h11 parse an attacker-supplied chunked message (default configuration, no special options).

finding.title: Symlink-following open with O_TRUNC in UnixFileLock truncates arbitrary files
finding.evidence: UnixFileLock._acquire (the default FileLock on POSIX) builds open_flags = os.O_RDWR | os.O_TRUNC (line 41), conditionally ORs in os.O_CREAT after a Path(self.lock_file).exists() check that itself follows symlinks (lines 42-43), then calls os.open(self.lock_file, open_flags, self._context.mode) at line 44 with no O_NOFOLLOW and no lstat/ownership check. Attacker input is the lock-file path: if the application places its lock in an attacker-writable/predictable location (shared temp dir, or a path the attacker can pre-create as a symlink), the open follows the link and O_TRUNC zeroes the target (or O_CREAT creates it) with the locking process's privileges, giving arbitrary file truncation/creation (integrity/availability, privilege escalation when the locking process is privileged). The stat-based pre-check in _util.raise_on_not_writable_file (line 22) is also a stat-then-open TOCTOU that follows symlinks and cannot prevent this; the identical unprotected O_RDWR|O_CREAT|O_TRUNC open exists in WindowsFileLock at filelock/_windows.py line 28. SoftFileLock is not affected because O_CREAT|O_EXCL refuses to follow symlinks, so only the hard-lock implementations lack the protection.

finding.title: Unix file lock follows symlinks and truncates/chmods arbitrary files at the lock path
finding.evidence: Attacker-controlled filesystem state reaches an unsafe file operation. UnixFileLock._acquire() builds open_flags = os.O_RDWR | os.O_TRUNC (filelock/_unix.py:41) and calls os.open(self.lock_file, open_flags, self._context.mode) at line 44. os.open follows symbolic links and O_TRUNC truncates the resolved file; no O_NOFOLLOW and no O_EXCL are used, and the only guard, Path(self.lock_file).exists() (line 42), also resolves symlinks and therefore cannot detect a planted link. When an attacker who can write to the directory holding the lock file pre-creates the lock-file name as a symlink to another file, the victim process opens and truncates that target and then line 46 os.fchmod(fd, self._context.mode) (default 0o644) rewrites its permission bits, giving arbitrary-file truncation (integrity/availability) and permission downgrade (confidentiality, e.g. a 0600 secret becoming world-readable) with the privileges of the locking process. The check at line 42 with a dangling symlink is worse still: O_CREAT is added and the path is created at the attacker-chosen link target. The identical O_TRUNC-without-O_NOFOLLOW pattern exists in WindowsFileLock._acquire (filelock/_windows.py:28). Required configuration: the lock file is placed in a directory an unprivileged attacker can write to (common when the lock lives in a shared temp/cache directory).

finding.title: SHA-256 circuit lets the prover choose the block count and never verifies SHA-256 padding, so `out` is not bound to the claimed message
finding.evidence: `paddedIn` and `paddedInLength` are prover-supplied signals. Sha256General (and Sha256Partial) derive `inBlockIndex <-- (paddedInLength >> 9)` at line 110 and only constrain `paddedInLength === inBlockIndex * 512` (line 111) plus `paddedInLength <= maxBitLength` via `bitLengthVerifier` (lines 125-128). These constraints only force `paddedInLength` to be a multiple of 512 that fits in the array; they never relate it to the message actually encoded in the blocks, and no constraint enforces that `paddedIn` contains a valid SHA-256 padding (the '1' bit, zero fill, and the 64-bit length field). The code explicitly acknowledges this, delegating the check to the caller (lines 130-131: 'we'll just do it outside the circuit'). Reachability/sink: all `maxBlocks` compressions are evaluated (lines 156-186), but the output is selected solely by `arraySelectors[k].index <== inBlockIndex - 1` (line 195), so the digest returned is the compression state after exactly `inBlockIndex` blocks and every trailing block is ignored. A malicious prover can therefore (a) freely choose which prefix's compression state becomes `out`, and (b) append arbitrary extra blocks after the hashed prefix, and (c) supply a block whose embedded 64-bit length disagrees with `paddedInLength`. The floorVerifier components that were meant to pin `inBlockIndex` to the floor are commented out and inert (lines 113-122), so the only active protections are the multiple-of-512 equality and the upper bound. Any verifier that trusts this circuit to validate the padded body/length instead of recomputing both outside the circuit accepts a proof of `out = SHA256(claimed bytes)` for content that was never hashed (truncation/extension of the message), breaking the integrity binding between message and digest and enabling authentication bypass in protocols built on Sha256Bytes/Sha256BytesPartial (which additionally forward the unconstrained `paddedInLength` signal at lines 19/33).

finding.title: ReDoS: developer-supplied RegExp run against attacker-controlled claims
finding.evidence: allowedAud/allowedIss/allowedSub/allowedJti/allowedNonce are turned into matchers by ensureStringClaimMatcher (line 39-53), which returns any object having a .test method unchanged (line 47-49) and never validates the pattern. At validation time validateClaimValues (line 154-162) executes allowed.some(a => a.test(v)) where v is the raw claim decoded straight from the untrusted token (line 210-212, 226). A catastrophically backtracking pattern such as /^(a+)+$/ plus a claim value like 'aaaa...a!' blocks the single Node event loop for seconds (exponential), a meaningful availability violation. No regex-complexity guard exists anywhere in this file; upstream added a safe-regex2 check (FAST_JWT_UNSAFE_REGEXP) precisely for this. Precondition: the app configures one of those options as a RegExp and a token carrying an attacker-influenced claim passes signature verification (line 188 runs before the validator loop at line 209), e.g. tokens minted by a third-party IdP or an app where claim values are user-controlled.

finding.title: Empty HMAC secret silently disables signature verification (unsigned tokens accepted)
finding.evidence: createVerifier only detects/prepares the key when it is truthy: line 399 is `if (key && keyType !== 'function')`, so an empty string (or zero-length Buffer) secret skips prepareKeyOrSecret and stays ''. At verifyToken line 180 hasKey is computed as `key instanceof Buffer ? key.length : !!key`, which is false for '' despite a secret being configured, so neither guard at lines 182-186 fires for a token whose signature segment is empty. Because the algorithm was explicitly supplied (e.g. algorithms: ['HS256']) the includes check at line 134 passes, and line 139 `if (signature && !verifySignature(...))` skips verification entirely for the empty signature. Result: a completely unsigned forged token (header.payload.) is accepted and its payload returned. The protection is absent: this version has no ensureSecretIsNotEmpty/-length check (upstream prepareKeyOrSecret now rejects empty secrets and prepareKeyOrSecret would otherwise produce a truthy KeyObject). Precondition: the app configures an empty secret together with an explicit algorithms list (env var unset, etc.).

finding.title: Cache serves expired tokens past exp when the token has no iat
finding.evidence: cacheSet bounds a cached payload by exp only inside `if (hasIat)` (line 89-102): when the token omits iat but includes exp, the exp cap at line 96-97 is never applied, cacheValue[2] remains 0 and line 104-106 sets it to the full maxTTL = clockTimestamp + clockTolerance + cacheTTL (default cacheTTL is 600000, line 384). min is also left 0. On the next verify call the cache-hit condition at line 262-269 matches (typeof value !== undefined, min === 0, and now <= max) and handleCachedResult at line 271 returns the cached payload directly, so verifyToken - including the exp validator built at line 452-460 and evaluated at line 209-228 - is never re-run. A token that carries exp but no iat (iat is optional per RFC 7519) therefore keeps authenticating for up to cacheTTL after its expiration. Upstream fixed this by always applying the exp/maxAge bounds into the cache entry regardless of iat. Precondition: the app enables the cache option.

finding.title: Double-drop in ThinVec::clear() when an element's Drop panics
finding.evidence: All of ThinVec's public API is safe Rust, so any caller can trigger this. clear() (src/lib.rs:1082) runs ptr::drop_in_place(&mut self[..]) at line 1084 and only afterwards resets the length with self.set_len(0) at line 1085. Element destructors are arbitrary user code and may panic (e.g. a destructor that panics on attacker-influenced state); when one does, unwinding skips line 1085, leaving the ThinVec reporting its original length. The value then unwinds through impl Drop for ThinVec (lines 1910-1930), whose drop_non_singleton again calls ptr::drop_in_place(&mut this[..]) over the whole (still non-zero) length (line 1917), re-dropping every element that was already destroyed. Dropping the same value twice corrupts memory (double free/use-after-free for elements owning resources) and is reachable with no unsafe code on the caller's side. There is no unwind guard (e.g. a DropGuard) keeping the length in a valid state before the panic escapes, so the protection that normally makes set_len(0) sufficient is defeated. Requires the default panic=unwind strategy. Upstream fixed exactly this in 0.2.16 (release notes: 'Fix two double-drop issues with ThinVec::clear() ... when the Drop implementation of the item panics').

finding.title: Double-drop in ThinVec IntoIter drop when an element's Drop panics
finding.evidence: Dropping a ThinVec iterator is safe Rust: let it = v.into_iter(); drop(it). IntoIter::drop (src/lib.rs:2539) calls drop_non_singleton (line 2544), which at line 2546 moves the buffer out with mem::replace(&mut this.vec, ThinVec::new()) into a local `vec`, calls ptr::drop_in_place(&mut vec[this.start..]) at line 2547, and only then clears the length via vec.set_len_non_singleton(0) at line 2548. If any item's destructor panics, line 2548 is skipped and unwinding drops the local `vec`; its length still spans the dropped range, so impl Drop for ThinVec runs ptr::drop_in_place(&mut this[..]) a second time (line 1917), destroying the same elements again. Elements that own heap memory or other resources are freed twice (double free/use-after-free); the caller needs no unsafe code, only a destructor that can panic. No unwind guard protects the length, and the panic=unwind default is required. Upstream fixed this in 0.2.16 (release notes: 'Fix two double-drop issues with ThinVec::clear() and ThinVec::into_iter() when the Drop implementation of the item panics').

finding.title: `ThinVec::clear()` double-drops elements when an element's `Drop` panics
finding.evidence: `clear()` (line 1082) runs `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut self[..])` (line 1084) over all `self.len()` elements and only afterwards resets the length with `self.set_len(0)` (line 1085). The input is any safe call to `clear()` on a `ThinVec<T>` whose element destructor can panic (a `T` carrying attacker-influenced state whose `Drop`/field drops unwrap, assert, or run panicking code). If the destructor of element i unwinds, control leaves `clear()` before line 1085, so the header still reports the old length while elements i..len have already been destroyed. The destructor runs a second time: either `Drop for ThinVec` on line 1917 (`ptr::drop_in_place(&mut this[..])`) fires while the owning frame unwinds, or any later `drop`/`clear`/`set_len`-based teardown re-drops the vector after a `catch_unwind`. That is a double free / use-after-free of the same values from 100% safe code (subsequent heap reuse of a `Box`/`String`/`Rc` element makes it exploitable). No protection is present: `clear` has no unwind guard, while the sibling `truncate` (lines 1061-1063) demonstrably decrements the length *before* each `drop_in_place` precisely to avoid re-dropping, and the upstream fix wraps this loop in a `DropGuard` that sets `len` to 0 on unwind. Required configuration: none (default features, safe API).

finding.title: `IntoIter::drop` double-drops remaining elements when an element's `Drop` panics
finding.evidence: `IntoIter::drop_non_singleton` (lines 2544-2549) does `let mut vec = mem::replace(&mut this.vec, ThinVec::new());` (2546), then `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut vec[this.start..])` (2547) and finally `vec.set_len_non_singleton(0)` (2548). Input: safe code that drops a partially consumed `IntoIter` (e.g. `let _ = v.into_iter().next();` or plain `drop(iter)`) where any not-yet-yielded element's `Drop` panics. The panicking destructor unwinds out of line 2547 before line 2548 runs, so `vec` still reports its original length; `vec` is a live local that is itself dropped during unwinding, invoking `Drop for ThinVec` (line 1917 `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut this[..])`) which walks `[0..len)` and drops every element in `[start..len)` a second time. The elements have already been destroyed, so this is a double free/use-after-free of the iterator's remaining elements, reachable from safe code with no `unsafe`. Protections: none; the length is only zeroed on the success path, and the upstream fix (a `DropGuard` that zeroes the length on unwind) is absent. Required configuration: none.

finding.title: `layout()` builds an invalid `Layout` via `from_size_align_unchecked`, so oversized capacities reach `alloc` unchecked
finding.evidence: `alloc_size` (lines 386-410) only validates `data_size + header_size + padding <= isize::MAX` (line 404-406), but `layout` (line 441) then constructs the allocation layout with `Layout::from_size_align_unchecked(alloc_size::<T>(cap), alloc_align::<T>())`, bypassing the additional `Layout` invariant that the size, rounded up to `align`, must not overflow `isize::MAX`. For `T = u8` and `cap = isize::MAX - 8`, `alloc_size` returns exactly `isize::MAX` (8-byte header, no padding) and `alloc_align` returns 8, so a `Layout { size: isize::MAX, align: 8 }` — a pair that `Layout::from_size_align(size, align)` rejects — is produced and handed to `alloc(layout)` at line 453 in `header_with_capacity`. Attacker-controlled capacity reaches this sink through public safe APIs: `ThinVec::with_capacity(cap)`, `reserve`/`reserve_exact`, `thin_vec![x; n]` (macro -> `resize` -> `reserve`), and `Extend`/`FromIterator`, where the iterator's `size_hint().0` is passed straight to `self.reserve(hint)` (lines 1972-1974) and thus to `with_capacity`/`set_len` paths; e.g. a deserializer or length-prefixed field that supplies the capacity. Consequence: documented UB from constructing and passing an invalid `Layout`; allocators that perform size+alignment arithmetic or round the size up can wrap to a small allocation while the vector records the enormous capacity, so later `push`/index writes overflow the undersized heap buffer (heap buffer overflow), and allocators that reject the size instead abort the process (availability). No guard exists in this version; the upstream fix replaces the unchecked constructor with `Layout::from_size_align(...).ok().unwrap_cap_overflow()` (panicking with 'capacity overflow'). Required configuration: none (default features).

finding.title: Chunked reader blindly discards 2 footer bytes instead of validating CRLF, causing HTTP request smuggling
finding.evidence:
Attacker-controlled input reaches ChunkedReader.__call__ via the chunked Transfer-Encoding body reader (READERS SEND_BODY['chunked']). After a chunk's data is consumed, line 197 sets `self._bytes_to_discard = 2`; lines 163-169 then take up to that many arbitrary bytes (`buf.maybe_extract_at_most`) and only decrement the counter (`self._bytes_to_discard -= len(data)`), never checking that the bytes equal the mandated chunk terminator CRLF. So any 2 bytes are accepted as the chunk footer. PoC run against the target: feeding `POST / HTTP/1.1 ... Transfer-Encoding: chunked

5
helloXX0

` (footer `XX` instead of CRLF) is accepted by h11 0.14.0, which returns Request, Data(b'hello'), EndOfMessage, i.e. it treats the malformed chunked message as a complete, valid body. The fixed implementation (0.16.0) instead stores the literal terminator and raises RemoteProtocolError('malformed chunk footer: bytearray(b'XX') (expected b'\r\n')') on the identical input. Because h11 (commonly used as a front-end/proxy parser) succeeds while a stricter peer rejects or frames these bytes differently, an attacker can desynchronize HTTP message boundaries and smuggle requests across h11-based front ends, violating message-framing integrity/authorization. The vulnerable code path requires only that the peer negotiate chunked transfer-encoding (attacker can always request it).

finding.title: Unvalidated Argon2 nb_blocks causes heap buffer overflow (out-of-bounds write)
finding.evidence: argon2i_32() copies the caller-supplied nb_blocks straight into config.nb_blocks (line 328) and never enforces Monocypher's documented requirement nb_blocks >= 8*nb_lanes (monocypher.h:160). Line 345 allocates malloc(nb_blocks*1024) and line 347 hands that pointer to crypto_argon2. Inside monocypher.c:752-754 crypto_argon2 recomputes lane_size=(nb_blocks/nb_lanes/4)*4; with the binding's hard-coded nb_lanes=1, nb_blocks=1 yields lane_size=0, yet monocypher.c:776-783 unconditionally fills the first two 1024-byte blocks via load64_le_buf(blocks[l*lane_size+i].a, hash_area, 128) (blk is 'typedef struct { u64 a[128]; }', monocypher.c:659, i.e. 1024 bytes), writing 2048 bytes into the 1024-byte allocation -> heap out-of-bounds write. nb_blocks=0 similarly writes two blocks into a zero/near-zero allocation, and monocypher.c:902 (blocks + lane_size - 1) underflows for any nb_blocks<4. The malloc result is never NULL-checked (lines 345-349), so a huge nb_blocks also becomes a NULL-pointer write. Reachable directly from Python, e.g. argon2i_32(1, 1, b'pw', b'salt').

finding.title: Unchecked BLAKE2b key length overflows fixed 128-byte stack buffer
finding.evidence: blake2b() (line 281) and Blake2b.__init__() (line 297) pass the caller-supplied key plus len(key) as key_size to monocypher's crypto_blake2b_keyed/keyed_init with no bound. Monocypher copies the key into a fixed-size stack buffer: monocypher.c:546-547 declares 'u8 key_block[128] = {0}' then COPY(key_block, key, key_size), where COPY is an unbounded byte loop (monocypher.c:65). key_size is never clamped (BLAKE2b keys are limited to 64 bytes), so any key longer than 128 bytes writes past key_block and corrupts the stack. Reachable from Python via blake2b(b'msg', key=b'A'*256) or Blake2b(key=b'A'*256).

finding.title: Missing length validation of fixed-size key/signature buffers yields out-of-bounds reads
finding.evidence: signature_check() forwards caller-supplied signature/public_key to crypto_eddsa_check, whose parameters are declared fixed-size 'const uint8_t signature[64]'/'public_key[32]' (line 111). Cython emits no size check for such array parameters: the generated code converts each argument with __Pyx_PyObject_AsUString (PyBytes_AS_STRING), so a short buffer makes crypto_eddsa_check read up to 64/32 bytes past the object. The same missing-validation pattern affects lock/unlock (key[32], nonce[24], mac[16]; lines 181/199), chacha20 (key[32]; line 267/269), key_exchange and compute_key_exchange_public_key (secret/public keys[32]; lines 362/375) and IncrementalAuthenticatedEncryption.lock; only the class __init__ and the elligator helpers validate length. An attacker who controls the length of key material parsed from untrusted input (e.g. a signature/public key from a network message) reaches the unguarded over-read, causing a crash or disclosure of adjacent heap memory.

finding.title: Unbounded BLAKE2b key length overflows monocypher stack buffer
finding.evidence: blake2b(msg, key) forwards len(key) directly to crypto_blake2b_keyed as key_size with no upper bound (line 281: crypto_blake2b_keyed(hash, len(hash), key, len(key), msg, len(msg))); Blake2b.__init__ likewise forwards len(key) to crypto_blake2b_keyed_init with no check (line 297). Monocypher's crypto_blake2b_keyed_init (monocypher.c:544-546) copies key_size bytes into the fixed stack array u8 key_block[128] using the non-bounded COPY() byte loop (FOR(_i_,0,size) ...), so any key longer than 128 bytes writes past key_block and corrupts adjacent stack data (saved registers/return address). The API documents only an 'optional 32-byte key' and performs no length validation, so where the key length/bytes are attacker-influenced this is a stack write primitive. Source-derived; no build/PoC was possible in this environment.

finding.title: Module-level AEAD/stream/key-exchange/signature functions omit fixed-length key, nonce and signature validation
finding.evidence: lock() passes key/nonce straight into crypto_aead_lock (line 181) and unlock() into crypto_aead_unlock (line 199) without asserting len(key)==32 or len(nonce)==24, although the C code unconditionally reads key[32] (crypto_chacha20_h load32_le_buf(key,8)) and nonce[24] (crypto_aead_init_x: COPY(ctx->nonce, nonce+16, 8)). The sibling class IncrementalAuthenticatedEncryption does enforce exactly these lengths (lines 214-218) and the 16-byte mac check (line 246), showing the validation is required but absent in the module-level path. The same omission lets chacha20() pass an unvalidated 32-byte key to crypto_chacha20_x/djb (lines 267/269), key_exchange() pass unvalidated 32-byte secrets to crypto_x25519 (line 375), and signature_check() pass an unvalidated 64-byte signature and 32-byte public key to crypto_eddsa_check (line 429) - the latter are directly attacker supplied in a verification path. A short buffer makes the C routines read past the Python object into adjacent heap memory (info leak into the crypto computation) and can segfault the interpreter.

finding.title: Unchecked malloc plus unvalidated nb_blocks yields NULL pointer dereference
finding.evidence: argon2i_32 allocates work_area = malloc((<size_t> nb_blocks) * 1024) and immediately hands it to crypto_argon2 (line 347) without a NULL check. nb_blocks is caller supplied and never bounds-checked (line 328: config.nb_blocks = nb_blocks), unlike the password/salt/key/ad sizes that are routed through _validate_u32 (lines 334-342). With a large attacker-influenced memory-cost parameter the allocation fails, and crypto_argon2 then initialises/hashes through the NULL work_area pointer, crashing the process (denial of service). Source-derived; no PoC executed.

finding.title: Prover-controlled padded length/block selection breaks the soundness of the SHA-256 output
finding.evidence: `Sha256General`/`Sha256Bytes` take `paddedIn` bits and `paddedInLength` as freestanding circuit inputs (sha.circom:18-19,96-97) and derive everything from them without validating that `paddedIn` is a valid SHA-256 padded encoding. The only relation enforced between the two inputs is `paddedInLength === inBlockIndex * 512` (line 111), together with `paddedInLength <= maxBitLength` (lines 125-128); the 0x80 terminator, the zero fill and the 64-bit message-length field of SHA-256 padding are never constrained - the code explicitly delegates that check to the caller (lines 130-131). The returned hash is then selected solely from the prover-supplied length: `arraySelectors[k].index <== inBlockIndex - 1` (line 195) with `out[k] <== arraySelectors[k].out` (line 196), i.e. `out` is the chaining value after exactly `inBlockIndex` compression blocks (chain built at lines 156-197). Consequently a malicious prover, who chooses `paddedInLength` (any multiple of 512 up to `maxBitLength`) and all `paddedIn` bits, can make the circuit certify an `out` that is the intermediate compression state of a prefix of the supplied data, or of bit strings that are not a padded message at all (e.g. by shortening `paddedInLength` so only the first block(s) are selected, or by putting an arbitrary length/padding tail in the last selected block). Any verifier that treats `Sha256Bytes`/`Sha256BytesPartial` as `out = SHA256(message)` is therefore bypassable, because these templates do not bind the declared length to the data that is actually hashed and do not check padding. `Sha256Partial`/`Sha256BytesPartial` repeat the identical unconstrained pattern at lines 233-234 and 292 (and additionally accept an entirely prover-chosen `preHash`, lines 51,67-74), so the same forgery applies to the partial-hash variant. Required configuration: any use of these templates as a hash primitive without an external padding/length check.

finding.title: Unvalidated paddedInLength lets prover force an out-of-range block index and a forged all-zero hash
finding.evidence: Attacker input: the prover supplies the private signals paddedIn[]/paddedInLength to Sha256General (used by Sha256Bytes). Flow: line 110 computes the witness inBlockIndex <-- (paddedInLength >> 9) and line 111 constrains paddedInLength === inBlockIndex*512, so inBlockIndex equals the number of 512-bit blocks and is fully attacker-chosen; the only width check is bitLengthVerifier (lines 125-128), which bounds paddedInLength only from ABOVE (paddedInLength <= maxBitLength). There is no lower bound, so paddedInLength = 0 (inBlockIndex = 0, paddedIn data entirely unaudited) is accepted. Unsafe operation: line 195 sets every selector index to arraySelectors[k].index <== inBlockIndex - 1, i.e. 0 - 1 = p-1 (a huge field element), and line 196 emits out[k] <== arraySelectors[k].out. Failed protection: ItemAtIndex (array.circom lines 25-28) is supposed to reject index >= maxBlocks via LessThan(bitLength) with lessThan.in[0] = index = p-1; but LessThan computes in[0]+2^n-in[1] modulo the BN254 prime, which for in[0] = p-1 wraps to 2^n - maxBlocks - 1 (< 2^n), a valid (n+1)-bit value whose top bit is 0, so lessThan.out === 1 is satisfied and the bounds check is silently bypassed. Because no eqs[i] can match the index p-1, CalculateTotal sums zeros and the circuit outputs out = 0 for arbitrary paddedIn. Consequence: a malicious prover can produce a satisfying witness/proof of `out = 0` (an all-zero hash) for a completely arbitrary input, and more generally can choose inBlockIndex (and therefore how many blocks the emitted hash covers) freely. Required configuration: paddedInLength must be prover-controlled rather than pinned by the verifier; the check is bypassed whenever paddedInLength is a multiple of 512 in [0, maxBitLength], most directly 0. Root cause: the length quantity that derives inBlockIndex is never validated against a lower bound/minimum block count before being turned into a selector index.
